in_text_mentions: term outcome, with a monocyclic course that enters a permanent remission with time. A small proportion of patients have an intermittent course, with relapses followed by periods of quiescence. In the remaining half of the patients, the disease pursues a more severe, persistent disease course. Among this unremitting subset, the sickest children have ongoing systemic symptoms, early destructive polyarthritis (Figure 2), growth failure, and are exposed to the serious side effects of corticosteroids. This particular disease phenotype represents the most disabling of all the different forms of JIA.

in_text_mentions: a day. The intermittent fever is generally accompanied by a typical, salmon pink-coloured rash, which commonly occurs on the trunk and proximal extremities and vanishes with the decline of the fever (Figure 1). Occasionally, polyarticular arthritis, including both large and small joints, may appear during the course of the disease (18). In general, systemic symptoms of fever and rash resolve after the emergence of polyarthritis, which makes distinguishing it from regular polyarticular JIA challenging (3). Fever and other systemic symptoms can persist for months but rarely longer than 6 months.

A: Caption and in-text identify this H&E bone-marrow biopsy as from a patient with new-onset systemic JIA and show hypercellular marrow with prominent nucleated erythroblasts and erythroid expansion; these hematologic findings are not in the allowed vocabulary, so they are recorded as proposed findings. B: The same systemic JIA bone-marrow figure shows CD163 immunostaining with brown CD163+ cells, some described as hemophagocytic; in-text links the CD163+ histiocyte expansion in these sJIA patients to early MAS, supporting attribution to systemic JIA while recognizing this is a complication-associated manifestation.

panels.figure_caption: Bone marrow biopsy from a patient with new-onset systemic JIA. (a) H&E staining showing hypercellular bone marrow with prominent accumulations of nucleated erythroblasts (arrows). (b) Immunostaining with monoclonal antibodies specific for CD163. Brown staining identifies CD163+ cells (some are hemophagocytic). CD163+ macrophages are very rare in a normal bone marrow (not shown).
in_text_mentions: In two of the patients included in this study, bone marrow biopsy was performed as a part of the initial diagnostic evaluation to rule out malignancy (these patients had relatively low Hb levels: 7.2 and 7.8 g/dl). Both patients were found to have hypercellular bone marrow with mild expansion of erythroid lineage (Figure 5). These patients also had moderate expansion of CD163+ histiocytes, a phenomenon viewed by some [7] as early stages of MAS.

A: Real-patient axial chest CT of patient 1 in an sJIA case series; the caption and in-text describe extensive bilateral pulmonary involvement with multiple parenchymal and interstitial lesions. Pulmonary involvement is a recognized but less common sJIA manifestation, so the panel is attributed to sJIA with moderate confidence; the finding is absent from the allowed vocabulary and is therefore placed in proposed_findings. B: Companion axial chest CT slice of patient 1 showing the same bilateral pulmonary parenchymal and interstitial lesions described in the caption and in-text; pulmonary involvement is a recognized but uncommon sJIA manifestation, hence variant typicality and moderate attribution confidence. C: Bilateral ankle plain radiographs of patient 5 showing symmetric soft tissue swelling with preserved joint surfaces and alignment, a classic plain-film appearance of symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis in sJIA. Admission vitals showed tachycardia (140 bpm) and hyperpyrexia (40.1 °C). Laboratory findings included persistent thrombocytosis (platelets: 598 × 109/L), leukocytosis (WBC: 14.64 × 109/L), profound hypoalbuminemia (28 g/L), and elevated polyclonal immunoglobulins (κ: 34.30 g/L, λ: 13.30 g/L). Autoimmune serologies (ANA, dsDNA, ENA) were negative. Repeat SPE/IFE (Figs. 1C & D) confirmed polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. PET/CT demonstrated generalized lymphadenopathy (Fig. 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal MRI of a human patient with sJIA (article title: bilateral brachial synovial cysts in systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis) showing bilateral brachial synovial cysts with irregular cystic fluid signals indicated by white arrows. This is a specific, captioned manifestation of the target disease. B: Axial T2-weighted MRI of the same sJIA patient showing bilateral brachial synovial cysts with hyperintense cystic fluid signals (red arrows), directly captioned as a manifestation of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis. C: Magnified MRI view of a synovial cyst from the same sJIA case, showing the irregular cystic fluid signal (white arrow) described in the caption; a real patient image showing the captioned disease manifestation.

in_text_mentions: d in the cysts appeared to communicate with the shoulder cavities. In addition, magnetic resonance imaging was performed for further evaluation of the cysts. Irregular cystic fluid signals (hyperintensity on T2‐weighted images) were observed in both shoulder joints, subcutaneous and muscle spaces of the upper arms with internal septation (Figure 2). The cysts were aspirated and cyst fluid from both sides was found to be very viscous with a lot of particulates in it. Bacterial culture was negative. Cell count and other component analyses could not be conducted due to the viscosity of the fluid.
